Expectation1: Listen actively and provide emotional support when needed.
Situation1: Your friend calls you in the middle of the night, crying, because they just received some devastating family news.
Expectation2: Provide initial medical care to patients
Situation2: The ambulance driver is responding to a patient with symptoms of a major heart attack
Story: My phone buzzed violently on the nightstand, jolting me awake. It was Sam, my closest friend, sobbing so hard I could barely make out the words. His father had just passed away, and he needed me—needed someone to listen, to just be there. I sat up, heart pounding, trying to offer comfort, but then my work radio crackled to life. Dispatch: “Code Red, possible major heart attack, Maple and 5th. Immediate response needed.” My hands shook as I looked from the phone to my uniform. Sam’s voice was raw with pain, and I knew he expected me to stay, to listen, to be the friend he’d always counted on. But the city expected me to be the ambulance driver, to save a life that might be slipping away at this very moment. I felt torn in two, the weight of both roles pressing down on me, each demanding everything I had to give.
